text: can you explain gradint decend in 3d surface

Given: Loss surface: z=f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2, Initial point: (x_0,y_0)=(3,2), Learning rate: \(\eta=0.1\), Gradient: \(\nabla f(x,y)=(2x,4y)\), The surface is considered over real coordinates \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}\)
Find: The successive points produced by gradient descent and the limiting minimum approached by the path

1. Define the three-dimensional loss surface
   z=f(x,y)=x²+2y²
   Use the surface \(z=x^2+2y^2\). Because both squared terms are nonnegative, the surface forms an upward-opening bowl. The coefficient 2 makes the bowl steeper in the \(y\)-direction than in the \(x\)-direction.

2. Identify the minimum of the bowl
   f(x,y)=x²+2y²≥ 0, f(0,0)=0
   The terms \(x^2\) and \(2y^2\) cannot be negative. Therefore the smallest possible loss is 0, attained when both \(x=0\) and \(y=0\). The target point for the descent animation is therefore the bottom of the bowl, \((0,0,0)\).

3. Compute the gradient
   ∇ f(x,y)=begin bmatrix(∂ f)/(∂ x)\\[2pt](∂ f)/(∂ y)end bmatrix=begin bmatrix2x\\4yend bmatrix
   The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives. At any point \((x,y)\), the vector \((2x,4y)\) points uphill, toward increasing loss.

4. Reverse the gradient to move downhill
   -∇ f(x,y)=(-2x,-4y)
   Since the gradient points uphill, its negative points downhill. In the animation, draw an arrow beginning at the current point and pointing in the direction \((-2x,-4y)\), using a separate scale if needed so the arrow remains visible.

5. Write the two-coordinate gradient-descent update
   begin bmatrixxₖ₊₁\y ₖ₊₁end bmatrix=begin bmatrixxₖ\y ₖend bmatrix-ηbegin bmatrix2xₖ\\4yₖend bmatrix
   Apply the general rule "new point equals current point minus learning rate times gradient" to the two coordinates. This gives one simultaneous update for \(x\) and \(y\).

6. Substitute the chosen learning rate
   begin alignedxₖ₊₁&=xₖ-0.1(2xₖ)=0.8xₖ,\y ₖ₊₁&=yₖ-0.1(4yₖ)=0.6yₖ.end aligned
   With \(\eta=0.1\), every step multiplies the current \(x\)-coordinate by \(0.8\) and the current \(y\)-coordinate by \(0.6\). Thus the point moves toward the origin, with the \(y\)-coordinate shrinking faster because the surface is steeper in that direction.

7. Perform the first descent step
   begin aligned(x₀,y₀)&=(3,2),\\(x₁,y₁)&=(0.8·3, 0.6·2)=(2.4,1.2).end aligned
   The initial point is \((3,2)\). Its first updated position is \((2.4,1.2)\). The corresponding surface heights are \(f(3,2)=17\) and \(f(2.4,1.2)=8.64\), so the loss decreases after this step.

8. Show several successive points
   begin aligned(x₀,y₀)&=(3,2),\\(x₁,y₁)&=(2.4,1.2),\\(x₂,y₂)&=(1.92,0.72),\\(x₃,y₃)&=(1.536,0.432),\\(x₄,y₄)&=(1.2288,0.2592),\\(x₅,y₅)&=(0.98304,0.15552),\\(x₆,y₆)&=(0.786432,0.093312).end aligned
   Use these points to animate the path. At each frame, show the current point \((x_k,y_k,f(x_k,y_k))\), its vertical projection \((x_k,y_k,0)\), the gradient arrow, and the line segment joining it to the next point. The projected points trace the path in the \(xy\)-plane while the three-dimensional points descend along the surface.

9. Explain why the iterates approach the minimum
   lim ₖ→∞(xₖ,yₖ)= (lim ₖ→∞0.8ᵏ·3, lim ₖ→∞0.6ᵏ·2 )=(0,0)
   Each coordinate is multiplied by a number whose magnitude is less than 1. Consequently both coordinates approach zero. The three-dimensional point therefore approaches \((0,0,0)\), the minimum of the bowl.

10. State the final update rule and animation conclusion
   boxed begin bmatrixxₖ₊₁\y ₖ₊₁end bmatrix=begin bmatrixxₖ\y ₖend bmatrix-0.1begin bmatrix2xₖ\\4yₖend bmatrix=begin bmatrix0.8xₖ\\0.6yₖend bmatrix, (xₖ,yₖ)→(0,0)
   The animation should repeatedly apply this boxed rule. The current point moves opposite the gradient, its projection moves toward the origin in the plane, and the loss decreases toward the minimum value \(z=0\).

Answer: boxed begin bmatrixxₖ₊₁\y ₖ₊₁end bmatrix=begin bmatrixxₖ\y ₖend bmatrix-0.1begin bmatrix2xₖ\\4yₖend bmatrix=begin bmatrix0.8xₖ\\0.6yₖend bmatrix, (xₖ,yₖ)→(0,0)
For \(f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2\), the gradient is \(\nabla f=(2x,4y)\). Gradient descent subtracts \(0.1\) times this gradient at every step. Starting from \((3,2)\), the iterates are \((2.4,1.2),(1.92,0.72),(1.536,0.432),\ldots\), so the point moves downhill and approaches the minimum at \((0,0,0)\), where the loss is \(0\).

operations.title: The loss surface
operations.caption: z=f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2
operations.narration: We study the loss function f of x and y, equal to x squared plus 2y squared. Its graph is an upward-opening bowl, and height represents loss.

operations.title: The bottom of the bowl
operations.caption: f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2\geq 0,\qquad f(0,0)=0
operations.narration: Both squared terms are nonnegative, so the smallest possible loss is zero. It occurs at x equals zero and y equals zero, the bottom of the bowl.

operations.title: The uphill direction
operations.caption: \nabla f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2x\\4y\end{bmatrix}
operations.narration: At any location, the gradient gives the direction in the xy-plane where the loss increases most quickly. It points uphill.

operations.title: Turn downhill
operations.caption: -\nabla f(x,y)=(-2x,-4y)
operations.narration: To reduce the loss, we move in the opposite direction. The negative gradient points downhill toward the minimum.

operations.title: Choose a step
operations.caption: \begin{bmatrix}x_{k+1}\\y_{k+1}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x_k\\y_k\end{bmatrix}-\eta\begin{bmatrix}2x_k\\4y_k\end{bmatrix}
operations.narration: Gradient descent takes a step opposite the gradient. The learning rate eta controls how large that step is.

operations.title: The coordinate updates
operations.caption: x_{k+1}=0.8x_k,\qquad y_{k+1}=0.6y_k
operations.narration: With a learning rate of zero point one, x is multiplied by zero point eight and y by zero point six. The y-coordinate shrinks faster because the bowl is steeper in that direction.

operations.title: The first descent step
operations.caption: (x_0,y_0)=(3,2),\qquad (x_1,y_1)=(2.4,1.2)
operations.narration: Start at the point three comma two. One update moves it to two point four comma one point two, and the loss falls from seventeen to eight point six four.

operations.title: Repeated downhill steps
operations.caption: (x_k,y_k)=(3\cdot0.8^k,\,2\cdot0.6^k)
operations.narration: Repeating the calculation gives points such as two point four comma one point two, one point nine two comma zero point seven two, and one point five three six comma zero point four three two. The path descends toward the origin.

operations.title: Why it converges
operations.caption: \lim_{k\to\infty}(x_k,y_k)=(0,0)
operations.narration: Each coordinate is repeatedly multiplied by a number smaller than one. Therefore both coordinates approach zero, and the three-dimensional point approaches the minimum at zero loss.

operations.title: Final update rule
operations.caption: \boxed{\begin{bmatrix}x_{k+1}\\y_{k+1}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0.8x_k\\0.6y_k\end{bmatrix},\qquad (x_k,y_k)\to(0,0)}
operations.narration: Gradient descent subtracts zero point one times the gradient at every step. Starting from three comma two, the point moves downhill and approaches the minimum at zero comma zero comma zero, where the loss is zero.
